title.en: The Earth Itself Danced: Huathiacuri Wins Every Contest
title.zh: 大地也隨之起舞:瓜提亞庫里連勝諸賽

texts.period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The rich brother-in-law, angry that the girl had been given to the ragged Huathiacuri, challenged him to contests. For drinking and dancing, Pariacaca turned himself into a dead huanacu on the road: a fox with its vixen came playing a flute of many pipes and carrying a jar of chicha, put down their burden to eat the huanacu, and fled when it revived with a great cry - so Huathiacuri carried off the jug, the drum and the flute. Entering the feast with his wife, at the first sound of her drum the whole earth began to shake as if keeping time to the music: 'not only the people but the earth itself danced'. He drank all they gave him without a sign of satiety, then poured round after round from the fox's jug, from which the chicha never failed, each drinker falling drunk in turn. For the next challenge Pariacaca dressed him in a shirt of snow; for the lion-skin contest he found a red lion-skin at a fountain, with a rainbow round the lion's head; and for the house-building contest, while the rich man's vassals laboured, in perfect silence an infinite number of birds, snakes and lizards completed Huathiacuri's house in the night. Next day, when llamas brought straw for the rival's roof, Huathiacuri stationed an oscollo (a wild cat) that shrieked so as to terrify the llamas into shaking off their loads.
summary.zh: 闊綽的內兄見妹子竟許配給衣衫襤褸的瓜提亞庫里,怒而設賽。先賽飲與舞:帕里亞卡卡化作道旁死駝馬;一對狐狸攜奇恰酒罐、吹多管竹笛而來,見死駝馬便放下酒罐鼓笛大嚼;駝馬忽醒,大吼一聲,狐狸倉皇逃竄——瓜提亞庫里遂得酒罐、鼓與笛。他攜妻赴宴,其妻鼓聲一響,大地竟隨節拍震動:「不但人們在跳舞,連大地也在跳舞。」闊佬灌他多少,他便喝多少,面不改色;再以狐罐斟酒回敬,罐中之酒永不見底,接連醉倒一片。次賽盛裝:其父帕里亞卡卡賜他一件「雪織之衫」。三賽獅皮:泉邊得赤色獅皮,獅首環繞彩虹。四賽築屋:闊佬奴僕雲集,一日將成;而瓜提亞庫里夜間得無數飛鳥、蛇、蜥蜴悄然協力,天亮屋成,觀者莫不驚異。翌日駝馬為對手馱草蓋頂,他遣一隻尖嘯的「奧斯科略」(野貓)埋伏途中,駝馬驚得拋棄草束,功虧一簣。

sensitivity.note: Contest cycle between the poor son of Pariacaca and the rich pretender; the dancing-earth and never-failing jug are classic trickster wonders.

passages.text: So Huathiacuri accepted the challenge, and posted off to his father Pariacaca, who told him to go to a neighbouring mountain, where he would turn into a dead huanacu. Next morning a fox with its vixen would come to the place, bringing a jar of chicha on her back, while the fox would have a flute of many pipes called astara... when they should see the dead huanacu on the road, they would not wish to lose the opportunity of filling their stomachs; and that they would put down the chicha, the drum, and the flute, and would begin to eat; that then he would come to himself and return to his own shape, and begin to cry aloud, at which the foxes would take to flight... and that he would then take the things they had left behind, and might be sure of victory in the challenge with his brother-in-law.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 5 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: While this was going on Huathiacuri entered with his wife, dancing with her, and she charging his cup and playing on a drum. At the first sound of her drum the whole earth began to shake, as if it was keeping time to the music, so that they had the advantage of the rich man, for not only the people but the earth itself danced. Then he rose and began to drink to those who were seated, his wife filling the cups with chicha from the fox's jug. They laughed, because they thought that before he had given cups to two of them the jug would be empty; but the chicha never failed, and each man that drank fell down in a state of intoxication.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 5 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Huathiacuri accepted this challenge also, and went for help to his father Pariacaca, who dressed him in a shirt of snow, and so he vanquished his brother-in-law once more. Then the brother-in-law challenged him once more, saying that people should now see who could enter the public square with the best lion-skin on his shoulders, for dancing. Huathiacuri went again to his father Pariacaca, who sent him to a fountain, where he said he would find a red lion-skin; and when he entered the square, men saw that there was a rainbow round the lion's head; so Huathiacuri again obtained a victory.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 5 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The rich man at once began to collect his numerous vassals, and in one day he had nearly finished the walls, while Huathiacuri, with only his wife to help him, had scarcely begun the foundations. During the night the work of the rich man was stopped, but not that of Huathiacuri: for, in perfect silence, an infinite number of birds, snakes, and lizards completed the work, so that in the morning the house was finished, and the rich man was vanquished, to the great wonder of all beholders. Then a great multitude of huanacus and vicuñas came next day laden with straw for the roof... But Huathiacuri ordered an animal that shrieks loudly, called oscollo, to station itself at a certain point; and it suddenly began to scream in such a way as to terrify the llamas, which shook off their loads, and all the straw was lost.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 5 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.language: Spanish record of a Quechua tradition
texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: The Stag That Ate People and the Stone with Her Feet in the Air
title.zh: 食人之鹿與頭足倒置之石

texts.period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: At the end of the competition Huathiacuri proposed a last challenge: who danced best in a blue shirt with a white cotton huara round the loins. The rich man appeared first in the proposed dress; then Huathiacuri, with a sudden shout, ran into the place where the other was dancing, and he, alarmed at the cry and the sudden rush, began to run - to give him more speed he turned, or was turned by Huathiacuri, into a deer. In this form he came to Anchicocha, where, when his wife saw it, she also rose up saying, 'Why do I remain here? I must go after my husband and die with him.' So she began to run after him, and Huathiacuri after both. At last Huathiacuri overtook the wife in Anchicocha, and said to her: 'Traitress! it is by your advice that your husband has challenged me to so many proofs... Now I will pay you for this by turning you into a stone, with your head on the ground and your feet in the air.' This happened as he said, and the stone is there to this day; the Indians go there to worship and to offer coca. Thus the woman was stopped; but the deer ran on and disappeared, and it maintained itself by eating people; but after some time the deer began to be eaten by men, and not men by deer.
summary.zh: 賽事之末,瓜提亞庫里提議最後一比:著藍衫、繫白棉腰布,看誰舞得最好。闊佬先著此服登場;瓜提亞庫里忽發一聲大喊,直衝其舞處。闊佬驚駭奔逃——為求其速,他自己、或說被瓜提亞庫里——化作一隻鹿。鹿逃至安奇科查,其妻望見,也起身說:「我留在此地作甚?我要追隨丈夫,與他同死!」拔腿便追,瓜提亞庫里隨後緊趕。終於在安奇科查追上其妻,喝道:「叛婦!是你唆使丈夫屢屢向我挑戰,百般試我耐性。今日便叫你變作一塊石頭:頭朝下,腳朝天!」言畢果然如此,那石至今猶在;印第安人常往拜祭,獻上古柯。婦人就此止步;而鹿繼續奔逃,從此絕跡,據說它曾以人為食;但不久之後,鹿反為人所獵,人不再是鹿的食物。

sensitivity.note: Punishment-transformations closing the contest cycle; the head-down stone is a named huaca of Anchicocha.

passages.text: He said to the rich man, 'Brother, now you have seen that I have agreed to everything that you have proposed. It is reasonable, therefore, that you should now do the same; and I propose that we should both see who dances best, in a blue shirt with a white cotton huara round the loins.' The rich man accepted the challenge, and, as usual, was the first to appear in the public square, in the proposed dress. Presently Huathiacuri also appeared, and, with a sudden shout, he ran into the place where the other was dancing; and he, alarmed at the cry and the sudden rush, began to run, insomuch as, to give him more speed, he turned, or was turned by Huathiacuri, into a deer.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 5 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: In this form he came to Anchicocha, where, when his wife saw it, she also rose up saying, 'Why do I remain here? I must go after my husband and die with him.' So she began to run after him, and Huathiacuri after both. At last Huathiacuri overtook the wife in Anchicocha, and said to her, 'Traitress! it is by your advice that your husband has challenged me to so many proofs, and has tried my patience in so many ways. Now I will pay you for this by turning you into a stone, with your head on the ground and your feet in the air.' This happened as he said, and the stone is there to this day; and the Indians go there to worship and to offer coca... Thus the woman was stopped; but the deer ran on and disappeared, and it maintained itself by eating people; but after some time the deer began to be eaten by men, and not men by deer.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 5 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Five Falcons, and the Flood That Took the False God to the Sea
title.zh: 五隼與洪水:假神葬身大海

region.en: Between Vicocha and Llantapa, river of Pachacamac (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 維科查與蘭塔帕之間、帕查卡馬克河畔(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: The five eggs in Condorcoto opened, and five falcons issued from them, who were presently turned into five men, who went about performing wonderful miracles. One was that the rich Indian who had pretended to be God perished: Pariacaca and the others raised a great storm and a flood which carried him and his house and wife and family away into the sea. The site of this man's house is between two very lofty mountains, the one called Vicocha, near the parish of Chorrillo, and the other Llantapa, in the parish of San Damian; and between them flows the river of Pachacamac. There was a sort of bridge, consisting of a great tree called pullao, forming a most beautiful arch from one hill to the other, where a great variety of parrots and other birds passed to and fro. All this was swept away by the flood.
summary.zh: 孔多爾科托的五枚蛋裂開,五隻隼破殼而出,頃刻化作五位男子,遍行世間,顯大神蹟。其一,便是那自稱為神的富人遭到了報應:帕里亞卡卡與諸兄弟興起狂風暴雨與洪水,把那富人連人帶宅、攜妻攜子,一併衝入大海。其宅舊址在兩座極高的山之間:一曰維科查,近喬里略教區;一曰蘭塔帕,在聖達米安教區;二山之間流著帕查卡馬克河。兩山之間曾橫著一株巨樹構成的「普利亞奧」天然拱橋,美不勝收,各色鸚鵡與飛鳥穿行其上。這一切都隨洪水而去。

sensitivity.note: The deluge that ends the false creator's reign; tagged flood for the deluge cluster.

passages.text: They say that those five eggs in Condorcoto, one of which contained Pariacaca, opened, and five falcons issued from them, who were presently turned into five men, who went about performing wonderful miracles; and one was that the rich Indian, whom we have mentioned as having pretended to be God, perished, because Pariacaca and the others raised a great storm and a flood which carried him and his house and wife and family away into the sea.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 5 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: The site of this man's house is between two very lofty mountains, the one called Vicocha, near the parish of Chorrillo, and the other Llantapa, in the parish of San Damian, and between them flows the river of Pachacamac. There was a sort of bridge, consisting of a great tree called pullao, forming a most beautiful arch from one hill to the other, where a great variety of parrots and other birds passed to and fro. All this was swept away by the flood.

title.en: The Cup That Saved a Village: Rain, Hail and White Stones on Huarochiri
title.zh: 一觴之恩:瓦羅奇里的雨雹飛石之災

region.zh: 瓦羅奇里上方馬特羅-科托峰(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: On his way from Condorcoto to the residence of Caruyuchu Huayallo, Pariacaca came to the village of Huagaihusa, at the bottom of the ravine where the river flows, where they were celebrating a great festival. He entered in the dress of a poor man and sat down at the end of all, as is the custom with those who are not invited; but no man drank to him nor gave him drink during the whole day. Seeing this, a girl was moved with pity, saying: 'How is it that no one gives a drink to this poor man?' and she put a good draught of chicha into one of those large white calabashes called putu, and took it to Pariacaca, who received it with thanks and told her she had gained his friendship. 'This is worth to you the same as your life, for at the end of five days wonderful things will happen in this place, and none of the inhabitants shall remain alive, for their neglect has enraged me. You must put yourself in safety on that day, with your children... but if you reveal this secret to any other inhabitant of the village, your death is also inevitable.' On the fifth day she went far away with her children, brothers and relations; the rest were still drinking and feasting when the enraged Pariacaca ascended the high mountain called Matro-coto which overhangs the village, below which there is another peak called Puipu-Huana. Then an enormous quantity of rain began to fall, with hail and yellow and white stones, which carried the village away into the sea, so that no man escaped. This flood is still a tradition among the people of Huarochiri, and some high banks were left which may be seen before arriving at the village.
summary.zh: 帕里亞卡卡自孔多爾科托前往卡魯尤丘-瓦亞約住地途中,來到溝底瓦加伊瓦薩村——其時村民正大設酒宴。他作窮人裝束入村,按不速之客之禮坐於末席;然而終日無人向他敬酒。一位姑娘心生憐憫:「怎麼沒人給這窮人斟酒?」便取白色大葫蘆「普圖」盛滿奇恰酒奉上。帕里亞卡卡受而謝之,說她已贏得他的友誼:「這一觴抵得上你的性命。五日之後,此地將有大變,居民無一得活——他們的怠慢激怒了我。到那天,你要帶著孩子自尋生路……但若將此秘洩與村中任何人,你的死期也一樣難逃。」第五日,她攜子女兄弟親戚遠走他鄉;村中其餘人仍沉酣宴飲。盛怒的帕里亞卡卡登上俯臨村莊的高峰馬特羅-科托(其下另有一峰名普伊普-瓜納),霎時大雨傾盆,冰雹與黃白飛石俱下,將全村捲入大海,無一人得免。此災至今仍是瓦羅奇里人的傳說;村前尚餘幾道高岸,即當年洪水之遺。

sensitivity.note: Hospitality-reward flood tale; the single cup motif parallels Sodom-type visitor tests.

passages.text: On his way from Condorcoto to the residence of Caruyuchu, he came to the place where now stands the village of Santa Maria de Jesus de Huarochiri... Here there was a village called Huagaihusa, where they were celebrating a great festival. Pariacaca entered the place, where all the people were drinking, in the dress of a poor man, and he sat down with the others, but at the end of all, as is the custom with those who are not invited. But no man drank to him nor gave him to drink during the whole day.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 6 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Seeing this, a girl was moved with pity and compassion, and she said, 'How is it that no one gives a drink to this poor man or takes any notice of him?' and she put a good draught of chicha into one of those large white calabashes called by the Indians putu, and took it to Pariacaca, who received it with thanks, and told her she had done a very good deed, and had gained his friendship. 'This is worth to you the same as your life, for at the end of five days wonderful things will happen in this place, and none of the inhabitants shall remain alive, for their neglect has enraged me. You must put yourself in safety on that day, with your children... but if you reveal this secret to any other inhabitant of the village, your death is also inevitable.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 6 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the fifth day she took good care to go far away from the village with her children, brothers, and relations; leaving the rest of the inhabitants off their guard, and still engaged in drinking and feasting. But the enraged Pariacaca had ascended a high mountain called Matro-coto, which overhangs the village of Huarochiri. Then an enormous quantity of rain began to fall, with hail and yellow and white stones, which carried the village away into the sea, so that no man escaped. This flood is still a tradition among the people of Huarochiri, and some high banks were left, which may be seen before arriving at the village.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 6 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

texts.language: Spanish record of a Quechua tradition
texts.canonical_translation: C. R. Markham, Narrative of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas (Hakluyt Society, 1873)

title.en: Choque Suso at the Head of the Canal: Love, Water and a Fox Engineer
title.zh: 渠首的喬克-蘇索:愛、水與狐工程師

region.en: Ayllu Copara lands, above San Lorenzo de Quinti (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 聖洛倫索-德-金蒂上方科帕拉世系之地(象徵性標記)

texts.period: Huarochiri manuscript collected by Francisco de Avila, 1608; publ. Markham 1873

source.work: Francisco de Avila, 'A Narrative of the Errors, False Gods and other Superstitions... of Huarochiri, Mama and Chaclla', in Narratives of the Rites and Laws of the Yncas, trans. C. R. Markham, Hakluyt Society, 1873

summary.en: Having crossed the river, Pariacaca travelled over the fields of the Ayllu Copara, which were in great want of water for irrigation. A very beautiful girl of that ayllu, seeing that the maize crop was drying up, began to weep at the small supply that came from the dam she had opened. Pariacaca, captivated by her charms, took off his yacolla or cloak and used it to stop up the drain she had made, then asked her in loving words why she wept. 'My father, I weep because this crop of maize will be lost for lack of water.' He replied that she had gained what he had lost - his love - and would make the dam yield more than enough. Choque-suso told him first to produce the water, and afterwards she would yield to his wishes: he opened the channel, such a quantity of water flowed out that it sufficed for the thirsty fields. He promised to conduct a channel from the river to irrigate all the farms, and ordered all the birds of the hills and trees to assemble, together with snakes, lizards, bears, lions and other animals, to remove the obstruction and widen the channel. The fox managed, by his cunning, to get the post of engineer, and carried the line of the canal to the spot just above the church of San Lorenzo; but a partridge came flying making a noise like Pich-pich, and the unconscious fox let the water flow off down the hill. The labourers were enraged, and ordered the snake to take the fox's place; but he did not perform the work so well, and the people to this day deplore that the fox should have been superseded - the broken course just above the church is the place where the fox let the water flow off, never since repaired. Having brought the water, Pariacaca besought the damsel to keep her promise; they went to the summit of rocks called Yanacaca, where he obtained his desires, and she was well repaid when she knew who he was. She would never let him go anywhere alone, and he took her to the head-works of the channel he had constructed for her love; there she felt a strong wish to remain, and she was converted into a stone, while Pariacaca went up the mountains. Thus Choque Suso was turned into a stone at the head of the channel, which is called Cocochalla. Above this channel there is another called Vim-lompa, where there is another stone, into which they say Coniraya was turned.
summary.zh: 帕里亞卡卡渡河之後,行經科帕拉世系的田畝——其時缺水甚急。田中有一極美的少女,眼見玉米將因缺水枯萎,對著自己開閘引來的涓涓細流哭泣。帕里亞卡卡為其姿色所動,脫下斗篷「亞科利亞」塞住她掘開的排水口,然後柔聲相問:「姑娘為何啼哭?」「父親,我哭這片玉米要旱死了。」他答道:「你已得到我失去的東西——我的愛。我必使閘中水足灌你的田。」喬克-蘇索卻道:先引水來,後允所請。他開閘放水,滔滔而下,旱田得潤。他又允諾開鑿一條大河渠道,灌溉全部田莊:召來山上林間所有的鳥,以及蛇、蜥蜴、熊、獅諸獸,移開阻水之壩,拓寬水道。狡狐以巧計謀得工程師之職,將渠線測至聖洛倫索教堂上方;不料一隻鷓鴣飛來,「畢!畢!」連聲啼叫,懵懂的狐狸竟讓水順坡流失。眾役大怒,改命蛇接替狐狸,但蛇做工程遠不如狐——至今人們猶為狐狸被撤而惋惜;教堂上方斷裂的渠線,便是狐狸放水的所在,從此無人修復。渠成之後,帕里亞卡卡求她履行前約;二人登上名為「亞納卡卡」(黑岩)的巖頂,他遂其所願,她亦知情後甘願相從。她寸步不離,他帶她到自己為愛而築的渠首;她便執意要留在此處——於是化作一塊石頭,帕里亞卡卡獨自上山而去。喬克-蘇索就此化為渠首之石,其地名「科科查利亞」。此渠之上另有一渠名「維姆-隆帕」,渠畔亦有一石,相傳是庫尼拉亞所化。

sensitivity.note: Irrigation-canal love myth; Choque Suso as canal-guardian stone matches the named huacas of the channel system still in use.

passages.text: Having crossed the river, Pariacaca travelled over the fields which now belong to the Ayllu Copara, and which then were in great want of water for irrigation. In those days there was a very beautiful girl belonging to the Ayllu Copara, who, seeing one day that the maize crop was drying up for want of water, began to weep at the small supply that came from one of the smaller dams she had opened. Pariacaca happened to be passing by, and, seeing her, he was captivated by her charms. He went to the dam, and taking off his yacolla or cloak, he used it to stop up the drain that the girl had made... and she, without knowing who he was, thus answered: 'My father, I weep because this crop of maize will be lost and is drying up for lack of water.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 7 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: He replied that she might console herself, for that she had gained what he had lost, namely, his love; and that he would make the dam yield more than enough water to irrigate her crop. Choque-suso told him first to produce the water in abundance, and that afterwards she promised willingly to yield to his wishes. Then he went up to the dam, and, on opening the channel, such a quantity of water flowed out, that it sufficed to irrigate the thirsty fields... He examined the country, to see whence he could draw the water; and observed that above the site of the present village of San Lorenzo a very small rill came from the ravine of Cocachalla... By opening this dam and leading the water onwards, it appeared to Pariacaca that it would reach the farms of the Ayllu Copara.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 7 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: So he ordered all the birds in those hills and trees to assemble, together with all the snakes, lizards, bears, lions, and other animals; and to remove the obstruction. This they did; and he then caused them to widen the channel and to make new channels until the water reached the farms. There was a discussion as to who should make the line for the channel... But the fox managed, by his cunning, to get the post of engineer; and he carried the line of the canal to the spot just above the present site of the church of San Lorenzo. Then a partridge came flying and making a noise like Pich-pich, and the unconscious fox let the water flow off down the hill. So the other labourers were enraged, and ordered the snake to take the fox's place... but the people to this day deplore that the fox should have been superseded, saying that the channel would have been higher up and better if this had not taken place.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 7 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.

passages.text: Having brought the water to irrigate the farms in the way that is still working, Pariacaca besought the damsel to keep her promise, and she consented with a good grace, but proposed that they should go to the summit of some rocks called Yanacaca. This they did, and there Pariacaca obtained his desires, and she was well repaid for her love when she knew who he was. She would never let him go anywhere alone... There she felt a strong wish to remain, and he again consented, so she was converted into a stone, while Pariacaca went up the mountains. Thus Choque Suso was turned into a stone at the head of the channel, which is called Cocochalla. Above this channel there is another called Vim-lompa, where there is another stone, into which they say Coniraya was turned.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Avila, Narrative of the Errors of Huarochiri, ch. 7 (Markham 1873); not verbatim.
